subtopic: HOUSING UNDER VETERANS LAND ACT-REPORTS TABLED-DRAINAGE, REPAIRS AND ADJUSTMENTS

speechtext:
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make which deals partly with government policy and partly with factual observations in connection with certain reports which I shall ask the permission of the house to table.
I wish to table the report on Veterans Land Act housing presented by Colonel C. E. Parish following an inspection which he carried out under authority of P.C. 76 of January 9, 1947; also separate reports by the deputy minister of the department and the director of the Veterans Land Act. These three gentlemen together made an inspection of a majority of the subdivision projects upon which houses were built by contract under the Veterans Land Act all across Canada.

Attached to the deputy minister's report is an additional report made by a British Columbia committee into the Braefoot project near Victoria. The decision to have this inquiry into the Braefoot project was made prior to the appointment of the committee of dominion-wide jurisdiction.
Hon. members will I think find in the reports information bearing out the statement which I gave the house the other day. There are defects, but as I previously stated all these defects can be corrected, and I have already given the house my assurance that the work will be done without cost to the veteran.
Hon. members will I believe readily understand the reasons why these houses, erected under conditions of the greatest urgency, now require minor repairs. The accomplishment in housing 2,600 veterans' families who otherwise would be living under conditions which cannot make for a proper home life in my opinion far outweighs any weaknesses which have been shown in this construction programme. The fact is that the department completed in one year 2,600 homes under the most difficult building conditions which this country has ever experienced. How outstanding was this achievement is best evidenced by the fact that in Canada today thousands of houses that have been under construction for months are still far from completion owing to lack of materials and the scarcity of the right type of labour.
Contrasting with the achievement of my department in pushing these 2,600 homes through to completion is the fact that in 1946 -and this is very important-private contractors embarked on 1,750 contracts for veterans under the Veterans Land Act. During the year they were able to complete only 224 of these.
My deputy minister has reported to me- and I am sure hon. members will be glad to hear this-the reception which he and other members of the investigating body met with in the homes they visited. Almost one hundred per cent of the wives and mothers were delighted with the accommodation provided.
Hon. members will be gratified to learn that every member of the inspection committee agrees that the houses on today's market represent-this is very important too; it is in the findings-fair value to the veterans. Colonel C. E. Parish, for instance, states specifically that it would be impossible for the veteran to find housing of equal value for the price he is now paying. Colonel Parish is an outstanding engineer of wide experience-in house building. He is also a member of the

______________Veterans Affairs-Housing
Canadian Legion advisory committee on housing. Colonel Parish has made a detailed analysis of the defects, -a, close and I think very fair analysis. That is what was asked for, and I can think of nobody in Canada better qualified to make such a report.
I should like to summarize Colonel Parish's recommendations. They are as follows:
1.	That the drainage problem be carefully studied and efficient drainage schemes provided without cost to the purchaser.
2.	That where sewage disposal is inefficient, correction be made by installation of new disposal fields or by connection to municipal sewerage systems.
3.	That structural defects be put into first class condition as quickly as possible, and that, where necessary, competent superintendents be retained to carry out this work efficiently.
4.	That the temporary softwood floors laid when hardwood flooring was unobtainable be replaced by suitable hardwood flooring when available.
5.	That no overall reduction in the selling price be made, but that the present policy of writing off costs owing to unusual conditions on a particular project be continued.
The deputy minister in his report recommends that an experienced drainage engineer, or engineers, be retained to supervise the carrying out of the recommendations in this regard. This will be done; in fact all necessary work and repairs will be closely supervised by officers of my department. In this connection I must point out that comprehensive action with regard to drainage cannot be undertaken until the frost is out of the ground.
While Colonel Parish and the deputy minister have hesitated somewhat to estimate the cost of the alterations, very largely because they consist of a multiplicity of detail, the director of the Veterans Land Act has recommended that an additional $500,000 be added to the million dollar fund set up a year ago for the purpose of writing off excessive costs where such were found. These recommendations as announced will be carried out.
I direct attention also to the findings of all three members of the committee that the costs encountered are reasonable and not out out of line with today's market and that Colonel Parish specifically recommends against any overall reduction in the selling prices.
In addition to the reports which I am now tabling, all three members of the committee brought back with them many field notes of observations made. These are, in cases, quite bulky and extensive as referred to in the 83166-1024
report of the deputy minister, Mr. Woods. These detailed notes will be of invaluable assistance as a guide to those who undertake the work which remains to be done and will be useful in supplying as far as possible further information that may be desired through questioning.
Once again, with the support of my colleagues, I wish to assure the house that the work recommended by this committee will be carried out as expeditiously as possible and with the firm purpose of ensuring that the veterans who purchase these houses shall come into possession of permanent houses of which they can be justly proud.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs):	Yesterday the
member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough) asked the following question, at page 1550 of I! ansard:
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Are veterans employed by the Department of Veterans Affairs being let out while others with no overseas veterans preference are being maintained on the staff? If so, what is the exact policy of the government in this regard?
I took the matter up with the department and have received the following answer:
With reference to the attached question by Mr. McCullough as to whether veterans in the employ of the department are being released whilst other persons with no veterans' preference are being retained, I have no hesitation in stating that this is incorrect.
The only reservation with this statement is with respect to stenographic staff, and in this regard I wish to state that any male stenographers with overseas service will be immediately employed by this department.
With respect to the department's policy in releasing staff, this is based on a directive issued by the civil service commission, circular letter 1945-12 of October 2, 1945, which states:
"The temporary employees selected for release should, in general, be chosen in the following order:
(a)	Persons whose services are not fully satisfactory.
(b)	Persons who are ready to accept retirement,
(c)	Casual part-time employees.
(d)	Persons above the normal retirement age.
(e)	Married women not dependent upon themselves for support.
(f)	Employees not entitled to preference for war service, et cetera, et cetera."
Our procedure in releasing staff is to have all our staff rated by a rating board comprising our senior officials in the district. We have brought into Ottawa for a course of training senior officials from all districts to instruct them in the procedure of rating employees.
If an employee is dissatisfied with his rating, he may appeal to the district administrator, who forwards his recommendation to head office. The overseas preference is observed in every case and I would welcome a statement of the particulars of a veteran who is being released while a person with no overseas preference is being retained.
Our staff now numbers over 20,000. We regret to have to reduce to the extent of 2,000 in the near future.
That is, a deduction of two thousand.
It is impossible for us to deal with the merits of each individual case in Ottawa and we have, therefore, been compelled to decentralize this work under the jurisdiction of our district administrators, but we have laid down principles based on the civil service directive and our own experience to govern our district administrators in this unpleasant task of staff reduction.
If my hon. friend knows of any cases I shall be glad to have him inform me.

The Liberals, backed by the Tories and the Social Crediters, do not believe in economic democracy.
That is a pretty broad categorical statement. Then he continued:	.
They are determined to hand back the direction of the economic life of this nation to the financial institutions, Aluminum Limited, Steel Company of Canada, Consolidated Mining and Smelting, International Nickel, Imperial Oil, and so on. Offsetting our political democracy, they are imposing an economic dictatorship which rests in the hands of a few hundred so-called big shots who direct big business. I do not pretend, Mr. Speaker, to speak for the Progressive Conservatives or for the Liberals, but I am going to speak in no uncertain terms for the Social Crediters of this country. I am going to say that the leader of the socialist party in making that statement was either wilfully ignorant of what we do propose or was deliberately attempting to mislead the public.
In the house last night the leader of the socialist party said this:
We cannot one day demand parity and orderly marketing, and the next day denounce public planning and controls, as steps towards regimentation and slavery, as my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low), did in this house during the debate on the address.
I wish to state that I have consistently denounced a policy of planned economy, because I am convinced that a policy of planned economy will inevitably lead to statism and dictatorship. I have never at any time denounced public planning. I have simply maintained that there is no such thing now possible as public planning. There could be public planning only under a system of finance that succeeds in getting purchasing power into the hands of all the consumers of Canada, and that ensures healthy competition in most fields of endeavour. Consumers under such circumstances could then be called public planners-but only then.
The trouble with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is that he has shifted his ground so often that not only is he confused, but he has so confused the people about what he means when he speaks of planned economy that they cannot follow him. He found that the people generally-and he found it some years ago-saw the danger in state planning, or in government planning, the terms which they were using then; so he shifted his ground to another term which he thought would be much more palatable to the people, with the result that now he calls it "public planning."
I should just like to know what is meant by planning and by controls. I am sure that all honest members in the house-and I am sure that most of them, indeed if not

all, are honest-will recognize that everything depends upon just how one defines the word "control" or the word "planning". No agreement is possible among us, as hon. members of the House of Commons, unless we are most careful to define our terms.
When the leader of the C.C.F. speaks about controls he means turning over to a government department or board or commission the power of absolute control over some phase or aspect of the national life. I do not think there is any question about that. It is true, and I grant him this, that he may hope that it could be done in a democratic way; but I must emphasize that to the extent that somebody else has the power of control over any aspect of your life, you are divested of that much of your freedom, and you are a slave to that person's will.
I believe it is perfectly correct to say that if one's life is to be controlled, it does not matter much who controls it. I cannot see that there is any virtue in being victimized by state officials rather than by privately controlled interests. I do not think there is any difference at all. And yet the advocates of state socialism, right here in this House of Commons, try to tell us that the regimented, planned and controlled state, under a vested interest of a political party seeking power, is democracy, while a regimented and controlled economy under private monopoly, which all talk so much about, is dictatorship.

I think that is perfectly correct. But the fact is that both systems I have mentioned are dictatorships, and I denounce them as such. If anything, in my opinion the regimented and planned state is even more of a dictatorship; for in the regimented and planned state the people are the absolute slaves of the state, and short of revolution and bloodshed they are helpless to do anything about it.
Actually there is no real difference between a state monopoly and a private monopoly, except that the state monopoly is much more powerful. We have witnessed that the ones in Germany, Italy and Russia, which are the perfect examples of completely planned economies, or completely controlled economies, are certainly much more ruthless than any private monopolies we have ever known about.
Bearing this in mind, let us take a brief look at the controversy about government controls. The present controls that the government have been using were imposed under wartime conditions to meet an emergency situation. Rents were controlled to prevent

landlords from taking advantage of the housing shortage to raise their rents and thereby reduce the standard of living of the people. Prices were rigidly controlled for the same reason. Wages were controlled so that workers could not demand higher pay, since under our present financial organization in Canada there would have resulted nothing but increased production costs and therefore higher prices to consumers. You can take these controls one by one, and you will find, if you examine them carefully, that their real purpose was either to restrict production of goods and services in this country, particularly goods for home consumption, or they were to bolster up a week and faulty system of finance.
On the one hand the controls may have been introduced for the purpose of restricting production of certain goods and services, especially those for home consumption, so that the maximum effort could be diverted into the production of materials for war. Now that the war is over, it can only be common sense, it seems to me, that the cure for the shortage of homes is not to continue indefinitely to control rents. The sensible cure is to embark upon an adequate programme of building of dwelling houses which will ensure all Canadian families having homes of their own. Similarly, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me foolish to continue a rigid control of prices which was an emergency measure designed mainly to restrict certain kinds of production. Rather it seems to me that by removing every possible barrier to it, production should be increased to the utmost in order that through competition to please consumers, the control of prices will be exercised by the people through the things they have to buy.
Instead of limiting 'wages or allowing prices to go on rising with every increase in wages, thereby offsetting any possible benefit that workers would otherwise receive, surely the sensible thing to do is to supplement wages by providing workers with social security incomes which do not form a charge on industrial costs. By doing this we also get away from the need for imposing on the people an intolerable burden of taxation which reduces their incomes, all so that the state can dole out grudging charity administered by a hard-boiled democracy.
It must be increasingly evident to all thinking Canadians that we have to get away from our present methods of doing some things. We all must admit that. Surely every straightthinking Canadian can see that it is the harsh taxation, the centralized state controls, the state imposed restrictions and the bureaucratic regimentations introduced under war conditions that have landed Great Britain, the

Emergency Powers
United States and Canada into the mess in which we are floundering today. I do not think there can be any question about that at all. If we continue to adopt that policy, surely it. can lead us only to disaster and dictatorship.
I should like for a moment to review the position which this Social Credit group took in November 1945 when bill 15 of that session was before the house. The government at that time took the position that if remaining controls were to be removed, chaotic conditions would result, prices would rise, and labour unrest would follow. In answer to that we pointed out that though the government had been warned repeatedly about these very dangers, they had persisted in remaining within the confines of a debt-creating system of finance which created for themselves the very problems which they were then seeking power to continue to control.
We further pointed out at that time that under a sound democratic and scientific system of finance, neither inflation nor deflation could threaten our economy. At the same time we admitted that it is a fact that under our present debt-ridden and restrictive money system both inflation and deflation, with all their disastrous consequences, did threaten our economy. But we said these dangers cannot be dealt with satisfactorily through controls that place in the hands of individuals great power over their fellow men, because, as the war has so definitely proved, when one control is introduced to cure human problems it inevitably creates other and more serious problems and leads from one control to another until you have nothing but a great network of controls. The only effective controls are those which are inherent in a justly scientific economic structure which by its very fairness and justice induces-mind you, Mr. Speaker, I say induces-the full support of all classes of the community and will be freely sustained without compulsion of any kind. That was the position we took.
We further granted at the same time that the government required to exercise a measure of control over price structures, foreign exchange, import and export of goods, rentals, and so on; but we did urge that the government abandon bureaucratic controls as rapidly as possible and concurrently introduce a system of automatic controls that would do a better job without endangering the freedom of individuals in this country.
Just here I want to remind hon. members that Social Crediters were the first in this house to advocate price controls as an alternative to taxation, before the war situation 83166-1034
became intense. The minister at that time said it would take a gestapo to enforce it. Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that it has not taken a gestapo to enforce it especially in that field wdiere the government introduced the compensated price discount system to the payment of milk subsidies. That is exactly the thing we have advocated for many years as a means of price control, and it was effective without a gestapo or horde of controllers.
Moreover, not only have Social Crediters consistently demanded a system of parity prices, which has been talked about so glibly, for all Canadians, but we have gone further and shown the government how it can get the money to establish that system without resorting to taxation, which is much more than the hon. leader of the socialist party in this house has ever done.

The hon. leader of the socialist party in this house has advocated parity of prices. That is quite true, but his smokescreen of vaporings about the advantages of social ownership has failed to hide the fact that he would depend upon heavy taxation to produce parity. I declare it as my opinion that a full parity price structure can never be secured for the people of Canada if it has to depend upon taxation applied by this parliament.
Where do we Social Crediters stand on this whole question of controls? Do Social Crediters advocate the immediate return to the laissez-faire of irresponsible enterprise of the pre-war years? The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said so. He has tried to make it appear to the Canadian people over the radio, as I have already said, and again in the house last night, that we favour throwing the people of Canada completely on the mercy of private interests who will be free to exploit them. This is sheer nonsense. Social Crediters have always advocated responsible enterprise, and we did so long before the hon. leader of the C.C.F. veered into that position from the pressure of public opinion. We acknowledge the necessity of safeguarding the welfare of the people and of providing them with adequate and effective protection against evil forces that may exploit them.

With us it is not a question of the need of controls; it is indeed a question of what kind of controls.
Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls which enhance the power of the state at the expense of the liberties of the individuals of Canada. We vigorously oppose all such controls as vest in hordes of insolent bureaucrats authority over every phase of the lives of the people. Rather do we urge that as rapidly as possible wartime bureaucratic controls be removed, be replaced immediately by a set of effective checks and balances inherent in a revitalized and reformed financial policy, and which automatically safeguard the whole political, economic, and moral welfare of our people. Every thinking person knows that substantia! reduction in taxation will open the floodgates to full production, which I think is the surest possible way to control the threat of inflation. Electoral reform to ensure continuous response to the will of the people by their elected representatives in parliament is the surest way to control the threat of rising state socialism and totalitarianism and to safeguard the freedom of the individual. Establishing a monetary authority charged by parliament with the responsibility of maintaining a constant balance between effective purchasing power in the hands of all the people and the total of goods and services available for sale, together with a condition of healthy competition in all fields, is a guarantee against deflation and in my judgment is the surest way to prevent the exploitation of the people by financial monopolies.
"Public planning" becomes a reality only when all of the people are able to exercise the economic vote through the dollars they have in their pockets to spend. These dollars arp their economic ballots through which they express their choices with regard to the kind of goods and services they want, with regard to the amount of these goods and services that they want, under what conditions they shall be delivered to them, who is to make them, and so on.
Again, application of the compensated price discount, which has been used by the government in its milk subsidies policy, is the surest and the safest way to control prices to consumers. We advocate that. '
Again, a system of subsidies, financed not out of taxation, but by the creation of new money, debt-free, to represent the goods and services that otherwise would be wasted in Canada, is the surest way to establish stability of wage scales and of commodity prices to primary producers. We have always thought that the government acted very unwisely in

dropping the subsidies on milk, and it would be equally unwise to drop the subsidies on cream. Through this action of the government a good many people will suffer a seriously depressed standard of living. I predict that the government will have to come back to these subsidies, and the sooner they do the more surely will they prevent serious deflation in this country in the years ahead.
All these things which I have outlined Social Crediters fight for and all of them are entirely practicable. They represent the only alternative to bureaucratic controls of the "planned" state on the one hand, and on the other the weak, ineffective, laissez-faire checks and balances of the present out-worn and irresponsible financial system which juggles so carelessly with human life, and which has plunged it periodically into depressions with all their hell of hunger, of nakedness and of economic insecurity. Social Crediters fight constantly for a revitalized democracy with all that that means, including economic democracy. I would say right here and now that the leader of the socialist party has no right to declare that this group has not fought for economic democracy. There can be no democracy at all without economic freedom. That is the very thing we have been advocating, and that is the thing which my hon. friend has only recently come to understand must be

us. If I speak at this moment, it is because I feel that I must explain the way I am going to vote. And I believe this explanation necessary because of the constitutional factor which consideration of the resolution injects into this matter.
It is evident that the bill which will follow the passing of the resolution, will impinge on the field of property and civil rights, which our constitution places under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, as stated in subsection 13, section 92 of the British North America Act.
The question that comes to mind is the following: From a constitutional viewpoint, are we authorized to pass such a resolution? If the answer is "Yes", as I believe it must be, on what principle are we to base our gesture? As a rule, when the federal parliament invade the field of property and civil rights, they justify their action on the basis of two different principles.
The first of these principles is that the government may, in the event of a national emergency and in order to provide against extreme cases of urgency such as those to which the war gave rise, pass temporary legislation even after the cessation of hostilities. The other principle was stated yesterday in this house by the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), in the following terms: the dominion may have the power even when there is no emergency to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, even though its legislation touches upon matters ordinarily regarded as solely within provincial jurisdiction. In other words, the judgment of the
I refer the house to page 1553 of Hansard:
And to supplement this expression of opinion which was formulated after that of the deputy minister of justice, may I quote the following from the legal opinion given by Mr. Varcoe:
(Text):
The true test, according to this decision, is whether the real subject matter of the act goes beyond local or provincial concern and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole. Such an act is within the competence of parliament though it may in another aspect touch upon matters especially reserved to the provinces.

Let us first consider the sources from which the first principle arises so as to ascertain whether we can admit it and subsequently rely on it to vote for this resolution. This principle, I repeat, is the following: In a national emergency, in order to meet extremely serious situations like those to which war gives rise,
the dominion government may enact legislation of a temporary character even after the end of hostilities.
This constitutional principle is admitted in all jurisprudence; it is clearly and definitely admitted in a recent judgment of the privy council in the reference on the Japanese question. That decision is based on the principles which the privy council had already enunciated in the case of the Fort Francis Pulp and Power Company Limited v. the Manitoba Free Press Company Limited. Here is what is said in Viscount Haldane's judgment:
(Text):
It is clear that in normal circumstances the dominion parliament could not have so legislated as to set up the machinery of control over the paper manufacturers which is now in question. The recent decision of the judicial committe in the Board of Commerce case, a well as earlier decisions show, that as the dominion parliament cannot ordinarly legislate so as to interfere with property and civil rights in the provinces, it could not have done rvhat the two statutes under consideration purport to do had the situation been normal. But it does not follow that in a very very different case, such as that of sudden danger to social order arising from the outbreak of the great war, the parliament of the dominion cannot act under other powers which may well be implied in the constitution.
Then a little later on:
The general control of property and civil rights for normal purposes remains with the provincial legislatures. But questions may arise by reason of the special circumstances of the national emergency which concerns nothing short of the peace, order and good government of Canada as a whole.
Then later:
Their lordships, therefore, entertain no doubt that however the wording of sections 94 and 92 may have laid down a framework under which, as a general principle, the dominion parliament is to be excluded from trenching on property and civil rights in the provinces of Canada, yet in a sufficiently great emergency such as that arising out of war, there is implied the power to deal adequately with that emergency for the safety of the dominion as a whole.

I now wish to discuss as briefly as possible the second principle which I mentioned at the beginning and under which some jurists would allow the government to encroach upon the exclusive rights of the provinces by claiming that the object of the legislation is peace, order and good government of the country, even if it deals with matters usually considered as subject to provincial jurisdiction only.
I respect the enlightened opinion formulated yesterday by the Minister of Justice, who also quoted his deputy minister, but I must say that I respectfully disagree with them on that point, and several of my colleagues have told me that they share my views on the matter. The Minister of Justice contends that the principle stated is based on a judgment rendered by the privy council in the Temperance Act case. That piece of legislation had been adopted by the Parliament of Canada in 1878 and had to do with the sale of alcoholic beverages. The validity of the act had been questioned in the case of Russell vs. the Queen, in 1882; however, the privy council had confirmed its validity. That very question was again raised regarding the same legislation in the recent case of the Attorney General of Ontario et al vs. the Canada Temperance Federation et al, brought before the privy council in 1946. Judgment was delivered on January 21, 1946, by Viscount Simon. It is contended that the principle I mentioned earlier and which was stated yesterday by the Minister of Justice, was enunciated in the said judgment. In my humble opinion, the decision 
rendered in 1878 in the Russell case was erroneous. Subsequent decisions by the privy council express opposite views. I will only mention two: the judgment on an appeal re the Board of Commerce Act; and the judgment delivered in the case of the Toronto Electric Commissioners vs. Snider.
In the first case, concerning the Board of. Commerce Act, judgment was delivered by Viscount Haldane. I wish to stress this point, since the part which I propose to quote from Viscount Haldane's decision is in direct contradiction, I submit respectfully, with the opinion expressed yesterday in this house by the Minister of Justice. I quote:
No doubt the initial words of section 9'1 of the British North America Act confer on the parliament of Canada power to deal with subjects which concern the dominion generally, provided that they are not withheld from the powers of that parliament to legislate, by any of the express heads of section 92, untrammelled by the enumeration of special heads in section 91. It may well be that the subjects of undue combination and hoarding are matters in which the dominion has a great practical interest. In special circumstances, such as those of a great war, such an interest might conceivably become of such paramount and overriding importance as to amount to what lies outside the heads in section 92, and is not covered by them. The decision in Russell v. The Queen (.1882) 7 App. Cas. 829 appears to recognize this as constitutionally possible, even in time of peace; but it is quite another matter to say that under normal circumstances general Canadian policy can justify interference, on such a scale as the statutes in controversy involve with the property and civil rights of the inhabitants of the provinces. It is to the legislatures of the provinces that the regulation and restriction of their civil rights have in general been exclusively confided, and as to these the provincial legislatures possess quasi-sovereign authority. It can, therefore, be onlv under necessity in highly exceptional circumstances such as cannot be assumed to exist in the present case that the liberty of the inhabitants of the provinces may be restricted by the parliament of Canada, and that the dominion can intervene in the interests of Canada as a whole in questions such as the present one.
In the case of Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider, Viscount Haldane again delivered judgment, referring to the case of Russell v. The Queen in the following terms:
It appears to their Lordships that it is not now open to them to treat Russell v. The Queen (7 App. Cas. 829) as having established the general principle that the mere fact that dominion legislation is for the general advantage of Canada, or is such that it will meet a mere want which is felt throughout the dominion, renders it competent if it cannot be brought within the heads enumerated specifically in section 91. Unless this is so, if the subject matter falls within any of the enumerated heads in section 92, such legislation belongs exclusively to provincial competency. No doubt there may be cases arising out of some extraordinary peril

Emergency Powers
to the national life of Canada, as a whole, such as the eases arising out of a war, where legislation is required of an order that passes beyond the heads of exclusive provincial competency.
In my opinion, both judgments formally contradict the judgment delivered in the Russell case and implicitly admit that the decision of 1878 was erroneous.
It is true, however, that in the judgment rendered by the Privy Council in 1946 on the validity of the Temperance Act, the Privy Council seems to confirm the opinion given in the Russell case; but if the judgment of Viscount Simon is carefully examined, it is seen that the original decision was reluctantly upheld, for a reason which I can better express by quoting an excerpt from the judgment:
(Text):
The appellants' first contention is that Russell's case (supra) was wrongly decided and ought to be overruled. Their lordships do not doubt that in tendering humble advice to His Majesty they are not absolutely bound by previous decisions of the board, as is the House of Lords by its own judgments. In ecclesiastical appeals, for instance, on more than one occasion, the board has tendered advice contrary to that given in a previous case, which further historical research has shown to have been wrong. But on constitutional questions it must be seldom indeed that the board would depart from a previous decision which it may be assumed will have been acted on both by governments and subjects. In the present case the decision now sought to be overruled has stood for over sixty years; the act has been put into operation for varying periods in many places in the dominions; under its provisions businesses must have been closed, fines and imprisonments for breaches of the act have been imposed and suffered.
(Translation):
Therefore it seems that if the Privy Council refused to reverse its former decision, it is because the judgment had been delivered a long time ago and the principles involved were considered as part of the constitution itself.
Therefore, this decision, merely because it confirms the judgment delivered in the Russell case, should not justify enunciating a principle as dangerous as that expressed yesterday by the Minister of Justice. I cannot admit that principle, and I repeat that if there were no emergency and if the proposed measure were not of a temporary nature, I could not support it.
In conclusion, may I emphasize that the existence of a state of emergency in another country, even though it may affect the economy of Canada, could not justify the adoption of legislation, even of a temporary nature, under the first principle which I have expounded, unless a state of emergency existed in our own country.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution, which provides for the continuation of certain orders and regulations for a limited period during the national emergency, is to my mind one of the most important to come before the house this session. It is because what I have to say has to do with the principle behind the whole measure that I wish to speak on the resolution rather than on the bill itself.
Before I come to the resolution I should like to make reference to the speech delivered earlier today by the leader of the Social Credit party. He began his speech by dealing with such things as ignorance and nonsense, and I think he is to be congratulated on the way he stuck to his point all through his speech. I do not know why the hon. member should make so much of what he considers to be the urge for regimentation coming from this part of the house. If he looks back to the record -and one does not need to go very far back- he will find that his friends in Alberta have been doing some things which to my mind bode ill for democracy in this country. I hold in my hand a clipping which I took from the press only this morning. It appeared in
Emergency Powers

the Globe and Mail, and the headline reads, "End present political parties, Alberta Social Credit urges." Then it goes on to say:
The annual report of the Alberta government's social credit board, released today, urges "abolition of political parties" . . .
Then it goes on to say why, and here is the most, intriguing part of the report. It not only would abolish the political party system as we know it, but they go on and say:
The board criticized the secret ballot and recommended its abolition in certain circumstances. All the board's recommendations are qualified with some such as abolition of the secret ballot based on establishment of a new economic system.
I do not know what kind of economic system we could envisage in this country which would require the abolition of the secret ballot. To me the secret ballot is the sacred part of our democracy, because when we can no longer express our opinions in times of election freely and without fear, we can no longer have a truly democratic parliament.
The press report goes on to say:
The report said the secret ballot enables a citizen to evade responsibility for his actions, adding when he votes for a candidate of a political party, he is also voting for the party platform.
That does not always hold good. The press report goes on:
The secret ballot, the report continued, gives the voter the opportunity to condemn later the actions of the government for which he voted.
That is the privilege which they would take away from the voter. Having once voted for a government or for a party to form a government, apparently this board thinks that the voter no longer has any right on any future occasion to reverse his decision and to vote his party out of power. That to my mind is a vicious principle to insert in any recommendation in any report.
While the hon. member was at the height of his oratory, he went on to say that he was for electoral reform, that he was in favour of making parliament more responsible to the people. He did not go on to say how he was going to do it, but if he were to follow the pattern that is apparently shaping in Alberta, we can see what he would have. I spoke of the social credit board, and the personnel of it is given. You will be surprised to find that the board is composed of four members of the Alberta legislature. There is a board made up of four persons elected by the people who now would deny to those same people the right to exercise their secret ballot to remove them from the office which they were given the honour to hold for the time being. The 
hon. member made some mention of insolent bureaucrats. If there is anything which can go farther in the way of insolence than what is suggested by that board made up of four elected representatives advocating that in the future the people should not have a secret ballot, then I do not know what it could be.
I do not want to go much farther in that direction, because I have other things to say; but I want to state clearly that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in his anxiety to attack the C.C.F., has exposed certain of his philosophy which does not look very democractic to me. He said that he denounced dictatorship. I congratulate him upon that. Why should he not denounce it? All of us in this chamber are against dictatorship. But when the province from which he comes, the only one which has a government of the same political persuasion as himself, has the temerity to set up a board of four of their elected representatives who have, to use his own words, the insolence to present a report of the kind to which I have referred, then I say he is not doing much to prevent the dictatorship which he fears.

I have quoted the parts of the report which have a bearing on what I have to say. If the hon. member wishes to

Emergency Powers
quote the rest of it he is welcome to the use of the clipping, which I have here. I did not rise to attack the Social Credit party, and said what I did only because they have made certain statements which needed to be elaborated upon.
Last evening, in my opinion the minister made one of the best speeches he has ever delivered in this house, and during the course of his remarks he brought out certain facts which should be seriously considered. He pointed out that at this time there was the danger of subscribing to the propaganda which seems to come to us so regularly, to the effect that all controls except rent control should be done away with. Yesterday the leader of our group placed on record the result of a Gallup poll taken early this year on the question of whether or not all controls should be removed, with the exception of control over rents. Two-thirds of those asked the question replied "no". I am not suggesting that such a poll is 100 per cent accurate, because we have to allow for its mechanics, but generally speaking I think it can be said that two-thirds or more of the people of this country are alarmed at the way in which the cost of living is rising.
When hon. members rise and say they would like to see the removal of all controls except those over rents, I think they are doing an injustice to public opinion in two respects. In the first place, it does not bear out what the public have expressed, when they have had an opportunity to do so. In the second place, if at this time it were possible to remove all controls except rent control I still would not be in favour of taking that action. Why should we penalize one sector of our population? Owners of homes who are under rent control are just as worthy as any other people in this country; so why should we make them an island in our price control system and say all controls will be removed, all other prices may rise as much as they like, but those who own property will still be subject to rent control? I cannot see the logic in a situation of that kind. I have also before me a number of statements made over the radio by Mr. Donald Gordon. I am not going to take time to quote them all, but this is part of one delivered on November 1, 1946, which I think should be considered:
People that want price increases sometimes suggest that removing the controls at this time would not result in any serious advance in the price level. That is sheer nonsense. That sort of view is the kind of logic used by an ostrich when he hides his head in the sand.
I believe there is a good deal of truth in that statement. We have only to ask ourselves why we have this propaganda at this time for the removal of price controls, in order to have
an answer to the question of whether or not prices would rise. If it is the opinion of those who are urging that price controls be removed that prices would not rise, then there would be no reason for them to ask for the removal of controls, because in that event price control would have nothing to do with their prices. Under the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board no one is prevented from selling at less than the ceiling price, but people are prevented from selling at more than ceiling prices. Therefore anyone who says the removal of price ceilings will not cause prices to increase should not advocate decontrol, because it would have no effect whatever on his prices.
Who wants decontrol? Well, at their meeting in Toronto on January 28, 1947, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association went on record as being totally opposed to price control, and other similar organizations have been sending their representations to members of the house. Hardly a day passes when letters do not arrive on our desks asking for decontrol in certain fields. When you examine them carefully you find that many of these persons and organizations asking for decontrol of their prices so that they may charge more for their products are still quite willing to have controls remain on the things they must buy in order to produce their products. You cannot have it both ways. I believe, if the government wishes to deal fairly and squarely with all segments of the population, controls must be administered fairly and squarely. There must not be any hit-or-miss system, allowing one industry or one group of industries to be decontrolled so that they can clean up on the prices caused by shortages while others have to take the consequences.
In this chamber it is hard to analyse accurately the feeling from time to time on price control, but as a general thing I believe it can be said that the group to which I have the honour to belong have taken a consistent stand that, as long as it is necessary for the administration of just prices, controls should be maintained in effect. On the other hand, members of the Progressive Conservative opposition have been fairly consistent in advocating decontrol. If you look back over * the record you will find that at least one hon. member when speaking in this house the other day, I believe it was the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Menary), made the statement-and the members of his party sitting around him applauded at the time- that in his opinion all controls except those over rents should be removed. He also said that was the opinion of his colleagues, and
Emergency Powers

I take it that represents the attitude of the Progressive Conservative group at the present time.

speechtext:
I presume I would be
out of order if I quoted from a former debate, but if my recollection is correct I believe my hon. friend used these words:	"I join with
my colleagues to urge that all controls except rent control be removed." If that is not the case I shall be glad to be corrected. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) , I believe during the same debate, also took a determined stand against any controls whatever, as did the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) and a few others. I am not trying to pick a quarrel with members of the opposition as to their intentions or desires. They have their opinion on this subject, and it is an earnest opinion which I respect. But I believe it is an opinion which, if carried out, would cause what the minister described last night as a gyrating price system in this country. If we followed their advice, not only would we have inflation in this country; we would have the anomaly of both inflation and deflation at the same time. We would have more than that. We would find it would be not only a matter of prices going up, but a matter of a breakdown in the distribution of articles for sale.
I am sometimes told by hon. members that the average small businessman is sick and tired of controls and wants to get rid of them. But if they were to examine what took place in the last five or six years; if they were to ask the average small merchant about the business he did in the last few years as compared with the five years prior to that, they would find that under the price control and ration system the average small merchant did exceedingly well. They would find, too, that today a great many of these small merchants are changing their minds about price control and rationing. They are beginning to realize that, had it not been for price control and control over the distribution of goods, thousands of them would have had to close their doors during the war, with nothing to sell because they would not have obtained the goods. The big industries, the chain stores, the big concerns next to the manufacturers would have had all the business at whatever prices they felt like charging, while the small businessmen, dependent upon certain regulations and con-

trols to see that all were treated fairly, would have been left with either nothing to sell or no one to sell it to.
The small businessman today realizes, too, that there is only a certain amount of purchasing power in the hands of his customer. And the average small merchant does not make his living by selling to the people in the high-income brackets. Those are the people who can afford to go other places to buy their goods. He makes his living from selling his product to the worker in the factory and in the mine, and by selling to the farmer, if he happens to be in a farming community. They are the people having modest incomes. If inflation starts in, and if their incomes are suddenly taken away from them in the form of inflation, purchasing power is cut in half, and the business of that merchant is also cut in half.
So that the average merchant today, after having studied the situation, and after having a slight flirtation with inflation, is finding that the honeymoon is over. He is finding today that, under price control; under a control of distribution, he did better than he ever did in any other period in the history of this country.
I would point out to the minister and the government the seriousness of the steps they are contemplating. It seems to me that what they are attempting to do is to follow out what they call orderly decontrol, a process which the minister said was the opposite of the boom-and-collapse system of decontrol. If that is what they are trying to do, then I am not altogether sure they are succeeding. All we have to do is to look over the papers from January 1, 1946, to January 1, 1947, and follow the news items announcing the different rises in prices, announcing the removal of ceilings, to see that the government policy of decontrol has not been one designed in the best interests of the average workingman in this country.
I do not need to quote many figures; the house will have plenty of them later. But just to give one example, in the period from January 1, 1946, to January 1, 1947, the increase in prices of agricultural products is shown as an index of 4-4, while the increase in manufactured products in the same period was 8-6. It will be noted that the second figure is almost twice as large as the first.
It cannot be called orderly decontrol when prices of manufactured products increased twice as much in the same period as did prices of farm products. We find today that many farm products are still under price control; and so long as that means stabilization the

Emergency Powers
farmers are not objecting to it. But while this is going on, the government is permitting others to get out from under the ceilings entirely, or to raise the ceiling to an extent where they make it almost impossible for the farmer to produce his goods, which are under control.
I want the government to realize, too, the effect of a headlong decontrol policy, such as is being advocated by the Progressive Conservative party, and which unfortunately the government is following to a large extent, upon old age pensioners, for example, and other people who are retired and living on pensions of some kind. They may be receiving railway pensions, or they may be people'with fixed incomes, who cannot go on strikes to raise the amount of their pensions or incomes, who cannot go into collective bargaining or come to the government and say, "You must increase our pension because the cost of living has gone up". They are people who are in a category who have to live on what they receive; and if their cost of living is doubled, then the government is cutting their cheques in half. Surely that is a mathematical statement which cannot be contradicted.
Then there is another class of people, sometimes referred to as white-collar workers. In that class would come civil servants, schoolteachers, clergymen and thousands upon thousands of others who are living or attempting to live on salaries which cannot be adjusted from month to month, or sometimes even from year to year, but whose salaries have been set over a period of time. These people find that, as the cost of living goes up, their purchasing power proportionately falls, and their standard of living is necessarily lowered by that amount.
I should like the government also to realize what it will mean to people in modest income brackets who invested their last dollar, so to speak, in victory bonds or war savings certificates. They bought their bonds in good faith during the war, many times having to spend more than they could afford in order to make the purchase, and put that money away. But they did it, first, because it was a patriotic duty, and, second, because they believed it was good business to have some money put away in order that they might, after the war was over, buy things which they could not get during the war.
It was good business, provided that conditions remained the same. But let us consider the person who bought a $100 victory bond in 1942 and put it away. Then in 1947 he decides to use that bond to buy a piece of furniture, or something else which he could not have
bought in 1942. He takes his $100 bond, cashes it, and finds that his $100 is worth only $75 or perhaps $66, because the price of the article he was going to buy has gone up to a point where the value of his bond is almost cut in half.
That is something else to which consideration should be given. Let us not forget, too, that we have heard representations about widows and orphans, and the effect of certain measures on their living. Widows, orphans and others in that category have never been given enough by way of allowances to bring them up even to an ordinary standard of living. They have been given allowances which permitted them what might be described as a subsistence standard of living. Today there does not seem to be anything on the horizon to show a general increase in allowances for widows and their children. Yet those people have to take the same amount of money, go out and try to buy food, clothing and all the other necessities of life, the prices of which in many instances have gone up fifty or sixty per cent, and in some instances seventy-five per cent. It is not fair to ask those people to do that.
Then we have our war veterans. When they were overseas many of them, in their slit trenches, dreamed dreams of successful businesses they were going to have in this country, or dreamed about the farms they were going to operate. But when they come back and see the rise in the cost of living, and the increased prices of materials which would be necessary to set them up in business or to operate their farms, they are becoming cynical and discouraged, and in some instances dispirited, because they find that their gratuities and their reestablishment credits do not go nearly as far as they had dreamed they would. Had they been warned that we would have inflation to this extent, the situation might have been different. But many of them came back, expecting in good faith that every dollar they received during their service would be worth a dollar in 1947. Today they are finding that is not so.
Many times we have heard in the house about the tremendous increase in the cost of building houses, in the cost of farm machinery, and so on. All those things are affecting directly, day by day, all the war veterans in this country. And taking all these things together, I do not see how we in this parliament, we, who were in a position to enhance our own remuneration without having to feel too keenly the effects of inflation, can advocate that controls be now lifted so that the law of supply and demand may take its course.
Emergency Powers

Surely those who talk about that law of supply and demand must realize that for every law that there is in that so-called law of supply and demand, there are thousands of economic lawyers who are ready to destroy it. Those who profess to believe in capitalism must admit that the objective of capitalism is not that of free competitive enterprise. It is to prevent as much as possible free competitive enterprise, in order to corner goods or prices in one's own particular field.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What dictionary did you get that out of? Where did the hon. member find that definition of capitalism?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Surely members of parliament do not have to speak in terms of dictionary definition in this house. If we have not learned anything in our lives from practical experience and common sense, definitions will do us no good. If the hon. member disagrees with my definition of capitalism I shall be happy if he has in his own mind a definition that suits him. He has only to read the McGregor report on monopolies and cartels and a lot of other documents along the same line to find out that what I am saying is perfectly correct. I think the mistake that we would be making if we attempted to depend on the law of supply and demand would be to assume that all people under that mythical law wrould have the same opportunity to take advantage of the law of supply and demand. But that is not so and in this country it never has been so. There may have been a time when free competitive enterprise existed and worked. If there was, it was for a brief period after the fall of feudalism. But so far as the economic system of this country is concerned, there has always been a tendency for those who have economic power to destroy competition and do away with free enterprise and, instead, build up monopolies. I am not saying that this is an immoral urge because, under the system under which we live, it is the proper thing to do. It is the very essence of capitalism to do away with your competitor. That makes you what they call a successful businessman, one who has succeeded in pushing other businessmen out of his field entirely.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are you a success?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If success were to be judged by the dollars I have accumulated I do not suppose I could be called successful. But I have always taken the view that there are other things in life besides dollars and cents.
I think the choice we shall have to make is between stabilization and profiteering. The
['Mr. Zaplitny.]
government is trying to steer a course, and truly it is a wondrous course, between those two points of view. Either we can have a system under which the law of supply and demand shall have full sway, as the Progressive Conservative party advocates, in which all persons will be thrown on the competitive market and the stronger ones win, those who are in a position to profiteer will do so and the others pay the shot, or we can have stabilization. But we cannot have both. The government will, I believe, find it increasingly necessary to establish stabilization if we are to have peace and prosperity in this country and realize the dreams we dreamed of during the war of the new social order which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) loved to talk about and which he warned us must be on its way before the war was over, that new social order that we continually heard about over the radio all during the war. The government will find themselves compelled to pull themselves away from the point of view expressed by my Progressive Conservative friends, even though they hold that point of view sincerely and with the best of intentions, because it was that same philosophy and point of view which flung the ship of state on the rocks in the dark thirties, and the same philosophy will again land us in the same place.
There are those who say that if controls were taken off we would have tremendous production and that inflation would be defeated because of the great production we would have, which would do away with the necessity for having any control. But let me quote from the report of the wartime prices and trade board for 1946, where at page 45 I find this:
It was hoped that these adjustments-
That is, adjustments in the prices on furniture.
-would promote increased production of lower price lines which had been disappearing from the market ... By the end of the year, the total - supply of household furniture had improved substantially. There was, however, a lack of balance in the supply since higher-priced lines were quite plentiful and lower-priced lines were often scarce or unobtainable.
Those who talk about production being increased through the removal of controls do not realize that those who are in the business of making profits are not interested primarily in production. Their interest primarily is in profits and they will produce those things on which they make the most profit, regardless of whether it is the type of things that are essential or whether they

Emergency Powere
are what the people want at that moment. They will even go to the extent of restricting production to keep their prices up.
The other day, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was making one of his usual good speeches and telling us that he was against the state going in for trade and against the powers the government was asking for, I picked up the Ottawa Journal and there saw a picture of a mountain of potatoes, several thousand bushels of them in the state of Maine being dumped because they were surplus production. While I was reading the news item accompanying the picture, the hon. member for Lake Centre was quoting the price of potatoes in Chicago at S2.70 a bushel. Surely that shows a weakness in the private enterprise system which my Progressive Conservative friends believe would be a cure-all. Here was a case where thousands and thousands of bushels of potatoes were being dumped, destroyed so that no one could make use of them, at the very time when food was urgently and desperately needed all across the world.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That was done by the United States government, was it not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is a good capitalist government, the kind of government my hon. friend would have in Canada if he had his way. I do not care whether it was done by the government or by anyone else. I say that the destruction of food at this time when people are dying of starvation, in Asia and in parts of Europe is immoral, un-Christian and everything else I could think of to call it.
When hon. gentlemen talk about free enterprise it is time that they realized, as the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) indicated last night, that however terrible they may consider government control, there is also such a thing as private control. Those who talk of free enterprise seem to think that if all government controls were removed we would have perfect freedom of enterprise in this country. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Under our capitalist system there is and always will be control of prices. Prices do not set themselves. In spite of all the talk of the law of supply and demand, someone is in control of the things we buy and sell, and we must take our choice between providing, through our elected representatives, democratic controls so that prices will have a fair relationship to one another and all classes of the people shall have all the freedom they want in carrying on their livelihood, provided that they do not encroach upon that of somebody else, and have stabilization of prices and the cost of living; and, on the other hand, taking
the lid off, as our Progressive Conservative friends would like us to do and have their mythical free enterprise, which actually would mean handing over our economy to those concerns which, during the hungry thirties, destroyed not only potatoes but wheat and coffee and live stock, which they burned or dumped over the cliff into the ocean in order to keep prices up. Those are the powers I am afraid of. Those are the powers which the hon. member for Lake Centre did not mention in his speech. He only shakes his finger at the government and says they are asking for very wide powers. Who else should have the power if not hon. members who are elected by the people? Surely, if we believe in democracy, then we believe in giving power with responsibility. What the hon. member wants, what the Progressive Conservatives want, is power without responsibility. They want to give power to du Pont, to the big corporations, to the International Nickel Company, to Falcon-bridge, so that they can manufacture nickel for the enemy.

I certainly am not quoting from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Last night the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had something to say on what now passes from C.C.F. lips under the euphonious phrase of "democratic planning". Actually it means socialistic planning. There was a time when the socialist party, the C.C.F., were a little more frank with their expressions than they are today. There was a time when they called by its true name the kind of planning that they are now calling by this euphonious title "democratic planning." They called it "socialist planning" in their Regina manifesto, the C.C.F. bible. And socialistic planning it is. That is precisely what the C.C.F. are calling for, socialism; and they have seen this, if they have seen nothing else, that between socialism and continued perpetuation of controls there is a bond of union which demonstrates that controls are of the essence of socialism. You could not have socialism without a network of controls. They are of the essence of socialism. Socialism does not work without controls imposed by those who think they are doing the planning, regulation and regimentation of the lives of the people.
Of what does this planning consist? Hon. members who espouse the cause of socialism keep parroting away about its being done in parliament. We who have sat in this parliament during the past two years know very well that the planning, where it is being done, is not done in parliament or by parliament. It is done by those who derive their power at the expense of parliament. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that this whole system of controls was built up during the war on one basis and one basis only, and that is by taking power from parliament, from the elected representatives of the people and vesting it in a group of people whom we call the cabinet, who then proceeded to delegate it to controllers. That is the way the planning was worked out, planning through controls, and
LMr. Fleming.!
that is the method by which socialism would be enforced in this country. It is perfectly idle for anybody to expect serious-minded people to believe that planning would be done in parliament. The kind of planning that our socialist friends want is the planning that would be done in the way in which it has been done in recent years, by taking power from parliament and putting.it in the hands of a group of people outside parliament and usually beyond the control of parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am glad to see that the hon. member is at least following what I am saying even if he may not understand it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As long as we have government by bureaucracy we shall have the same excuses that have been resorted to by the government in recent years. What I do say is that unfortunately the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has not seen that what he is advocating will lead inevitably to totalitarianism, if pressed to its logical conclusion. It cannot do otherwise. That is the way it began in Russia: a moderate government to begin with, having a leaning to socialism, but it did not last long. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext:

him where Russia went in 1917, where Germany went in 1934 and where Italy went in the twenties.
It is unfortunate that the hon. member does not realize it, but the fact is that what he is advocating would lead eventually to that length. Apparently the hon. member does not realize that is the road which he is advocating should be taken. I do not suggest that he advocates communism at one jump. No. But he has not seen nor has his leader seen that the things they are advocating, when pressed to their logical conclusion, will lead eventually to despotism, because despotism is the essence of the system they are advocating.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I hope the members of this house have begun to realize that, next to the common sense of the people themselves, confederation is the strongest bulwark we have in this country against socialism, and that is the reason why the socialist party in this house is continually advocating policies that would mean the centralization of power in the hands of a bureaucracy at Ottawa, at the expense of confederation and at the expense of the provinces.

We shall not forget, I trust, the ready way in which the socialist party rallied to the support of the government last year when they resorted to a method of amendment of the British North America Act, which we of this party said was fraught with the utmost danger and would open the way to depriving minorities of their guarantees under the constitution. The policy that Lapointe preached, Lapointe whom hon. members opposite claim to follow, whose titles they possess, but not his principles

Amid all the contradictions in that speech, and in C.C.F. statements and policies, it is interesting to hear the leader of the C.C.F. using an expression like that. I might liken it, when he is directing it to the government, to the pot calling the kettle black.
What is the essence of it, this matter of not having it both ways? It means, Mr. Speaker, that when the C.C.F. party deplore the decontrol that has proceeded thus far they are deploring the end of wage control. It means that they are deploring the end of salary control, because those are two important steps, belated steps, taken in the direction of decontrol. They were taken only on November 30 of last year.
Now the leader of the C.C.F. cannot have his cake and eat it. He cannot have it both ways, and in protesting against the decontrol that has proceeded thus far he is telling the government that it must go back and reimpose wage control and salary control. There is no escape from that. He knows perfectly well, and his own followers have admitted it, that you cannot have a system of widespread price control without control of wages and salaries. Let him rise in his place, or let any follower of his rise in his place in this house today and say frankly that he advocates the reimposition of wage controls and salary controls. Let him be consistent and frank and say that. He will not dare to. There is not a member of the socialist party in this house who will today rise in his place and say frankly and honestly that he advocates the reimposition of wage control and salary control.
We have witnessed a very good example of double-talk. You cannot have it both ways.

They cannot have it both ways.
Some tears were shed by an hon. member, one of the socialist members, on behalf of the white-collar workers of the country. Well, I should like to see that hon. member, instead of trying to have it both ways, be frank and consistent and say that what he is advocating means the reimposition of salary controls. The class who suffered most in the country during the war was, I believe, the white-coliar class, the people ground between the upper and the nether millstones-on the one hand, high taxes and rising cost of living and, on the other, fixed salary ceilings without any escape from them. The hon. member for Dauphin apparently wants to put the white-collar workers of the country back in that strait-jacket. There is a fine sample of socialist regimentation.
Of course hon. members will recall that he had something to say on behalf of the people who are living on fixed incomes and the people who are drawing interest. It is strange that he did not choke on those words. I have before me this Regina manifesto of the C.C.F. The C.C.F. proposes that in future no public financing shall be permitted which facilitates the perpetuation of the parasitic interestreceiving class.

And so on. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we would see proper application of the Combines Investigation Act. Let us have a little wholesome sincerity and honesty and frankness in this matter. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I admire the hon. member's impatience; it is a pleasure to see him roused into doing something. At page 1583 of Hansard for yesterday, the Minister of Justice had this to say on this subject:
Only the extreme nature of the emergency with which the country was faced justified the vesting of such powers in the executive . . .
He was referring to these sweeping powers vested in the executive to control almost

Emergency Powers
everything in the country. By parity of reasoning I suggest that it is only by reason of the existence of an extreme emergency that the continuance of such powers can be justified. The emergency does exist in certain fields; of course it does. Accordingly certain controls will need to be continued as long as the extreme nature of the emergency continues, to use the words of the minister. But it is high time we did away with a lot of these controls that do not come under that definition, and it is about time we had some regard-the government, especially, and those whom they have placed in charge of the administration of controls-for the essential relationship of this problem to the problem of production. Times without number we have heard from the government that the danger existing today, the danger against which they require these extraordinary powers from parliament, is the danger of inflation. There is no great secret as to how this danger of inflation arises. It is created by the lack of goods in proportion to the available consuming and purchasing power. How are we to arrive at a solution of this problem? The C.C.F. really do not want the problem solved; they want the controls continued. Anything that points to the existence of an emergency lends weight to their argument that controls should continue. They are not interested in seeing the end of emergent conditions; as a matter of fact they do not see the difference between emergent conditions and conditions that are not emergent. They want the controls to continue permanently. Surely, however, it is high time we gave a great deal more regard in this country and in this parliament to measures that will have the effect of increasing and encouraging production rather than those simply concerned with the rationing of scarcity. We need to do a great deal at this session of the house in the direction of encouraging production, and one means that must be put into effect, before this house concludes this session, is a substantial and material reduction in taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I have time to add just one word in conclusion. At the appropriate stage we shall have more to say concerning our views on specific orders contained in this volume which I have no doubt will go down in history as the Heinz bill. We do not have anyone in this house by the name of Heinz; but I believe this bill, with its fifty-seven orders in council, all different, is likely to go down in history as the Heinz or pickle bill. We are confronted at the present time with a curious situation. We of the Progressive Conservative party, the official opposition, have done our best to contribute to an orderly
approach to a review of this problem. Last night the Minister of Justice asked that we defer discussion of the resolution; I took his suggestion to mean that we might seek information in committee, but that we reserve our principal contributions to the debate until second reading of the bill is moved. I wish to make it perfectly clear that, in doing what we have done in trying to assist the minister, we have made the only contribution that lay within our power to bring order out of the chaos that has been created by the procedure the government has followed. By bulking all these measures in one bill-a whole session's legislation, as was pointed out last evening by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)-it is going to be difficult to carry on an intelligent discussion of the various measures. It will be difficult to carry on any successful questioning in committee of the ministers concerned with these resolutions, when you have fifty-seven different measures all rolled into one. But that is the way the government has chosen. It is an awkward method, just about as chaotic as anything could be; but then what could we expect?
