speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) regarding the report of the Alberta government social credit board, published in the Toronto Globe and Mail, make me feel that the people throughout Canada and the world who will read Hansard have a right to know what is in that press report. Therefore I should like to have the privilege of reading it into Hansard, so that everyone may know just how bad or good it is. The article appears in the March 21 issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail, at the bottom of page 1. It is headed "End present political parties, Alberta social credit urges." And then follows:
Edmonton, March 20 (CP).-The annua] report of the Alberta government's social credit board, released today, urges "abolition of political parties dominated at the top as we know them today" and establishment of "unions of voters" which would control the actions of their elected representatives.
The board criticized the secret ballot and recommended its abolition in certain circumstances. All the board's recommendations are qualified with some such as abolition of the secret ballot based on establishment of a new economic system.
IMr. Fleming.!
The board is composed of four members of the legislature-A. V. Boureier, Lac Ste. Anne, chairman; N. B. James, Edmonton, secretary; William Tomyn, Willingdon; and F. M. Baker, Clover Bar.
The report said the secret ballot enables a citizen to evade responsibilities for his actions, adding when he votes for a candidate of a political party, he is also voting for the party platform. The secret ballot, the report continued, gives the voter the opportunity to condemn later the actions of the government for which he voted.
"The political party system makes it very difficult for the people to exercise their democratic privileges and assume their personal responsibility, even if they were so inclined," the report said.
The board reported "the obvious remedy for the evils of party politics is the abolition of political parties dominated at the top as we know them today," and adds "in Canada we have never had an unfettered parliament subservient to the will of the people."
I think it is only just that the whole of the ugly truth should be placed on Hansard, so that each person can form his own opinion. I believe it would be well to comment briefly on one or two matters in this report, so as to help everybody to understand the point of view of the people who made this recommendation.
First, let me point out that the social credit board is only a special committee appointed by the Alberta legislature to examine into and make a report respecting certain problems. It does not indicate that the government has accepted the report, that the cabinet has accepted it, or that the social credit league in Alberta or throughout Canada -would accept it. It is merely a report and recommendation, probably purely philosophic and scientific and perhaps not to be adopted for a good long time if ever into the actual and practical political activities of the country.
In the first paragraph hon. members will note that these words are quoted:
"Abolition of political parties dominated at the top as we know them today."
The essential words are "dominated at the top as we know them today." I would probably be out of order in what I am now about to say if I were not discussing orders in council of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). But I will just call the attention of hon. members to the absolutely indefensible policy which has obtained in Canada in respect of beet sugar production during the war. And I will ask hon. members to tell me whether they think the Liberal government which has been in power, and has been administering that policy, has been free to do the thing it thought best, in the interests of Canada, or whether it has been influenced by

Emergency Powers
certain bodies of people who perhaps contributed to the slush fund or election funds of the party which is in power. Mr. Speaker, first I wish to pay a special tribute to the former Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) and the officers of his control board with whom I have had a great deal of correspondence during the war and since. I have always found the minister very attentive, patient and courteous with regard to any complaints made and I believe that he and his staff have carried out their duties with zeal and diligence in a difficult situation to the best of their ability. The situation with which they were faced was one in which business generally throughout Canada was upset by so great a wTar, and in addition we had problems in domestic and foreign affairs.
Coming now to the resolution, I believe that the discussion on the bill itself will be shortened by the statements which have been made by the minister and the various other speakers. I come from a large industrial city where we have been very much affected by the continuation now, for nearly two years-after the war, of a vast control system. The Canadian people have, I believe, been long-suffering under these controls, but they have about reached the limit of their patience and I trust that the minister, when he tables the various orders in council, will give some further explanation of the necessity of these controls.
Business large and small in this country, as; you know, Mr. Speaker, from your knowledge of your own great city, has been clamouring for freedom from so many controls. With the-

Emergency Powers
overtaxation, overgovernment and the failure to eliminate some of these somewhat minor controls, the smaller businessmen are finding it very hard to continue. They are hamstrung and interfered with in the conduct of their business from the commercial aspect.
I do not wish to go into the matters which the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) dealt with so ably last night, but I wish to point out one or two things with regard to the policy of the government in domestic matters as I see it.
As I see it, the policy of the government in domestic matters since the war ended almost two years ago is menacing to anybody who wanted to see controls eliminated. So far as I see it, the balance of the controls are not placed on any definite settled principle. The government are operating with none of these principles to guide them after the 15th of May. They do not indicate what one can expect from the ministry to clear the way after May 15. The whole story at home is one of the greatest menaces that we have. What are these orders in council that are to be enforced until May 15? Once they have this system, they find it difficult to get away from it. Those who are in charge of the controls think that, they are indispensable, that the country cannot get on without them. Unless price control is unified with wage control, it leads to inflation and no control at all.
Since the war closed, the board has been seeking to control every walk of life and almost every commodity, over parliament's head and without any responsible action by a minister of the crown to interfere with it. The minister never even sees the speeches. These officials just issue them over the heads of the ministers. The people of this country are long suffering, but there is a limit to their patience and it has now been overreached.
Since the war closed, the board has hamstrung almost every private business. It is interfering with those who are trying to conduct their business. As I see it, at the present time there is virtually no control on all kinds of bodies that are spending a great deal of money over the head of parliament. Every principle for which the British nation struggled in the old land since the seventeenth century has been surrendered to political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxes shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
I wish to emphasize to the house that the powers of legislation, even older than the right of taxpayers to determine the national
expenditures, have been surrendered and, if we are to continue this sort of thing, the power of parliament will be gone forever. Whole spheres of activity involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal. I wish to object to that as I have done before. We are told that parliament is supreme. Why does it allow all this to go on and even pass the expenditures?
The story so far as I can see is this, that the government instead of lessening controls and giving the industrialists a freer hand, is retaining controls and adding to them. This reacts on the small business man. He has to make out reports and papers, and that all interferes with his business. Firms are hamstrung in their business, and it makes the task of true recovery most embarrassing and difficult. The doubts, uncertainties and fears which are being engendered in the minds of the small and large businessmen in the management of their industries great and small affects them adversely, with the heavy taxes and restraints. So far as private enterprise and private initiative are concerned, they have never had a chance in Canada since the war has ended. This condition of affairs is sapping the energy of many businessmen. The control system is becoming heavy and laborious on the people. So far as the businessman is concerned we have seen the result of all this on taxation. This country has squandered its natural resources for many years, so much so that we are heading for a financial disaster. With the heavy taxation, with the burden of debt on the people and all that kind of thing we have squandered our resources at a rapid pace, and generations yet unborn will be taxed for it all.
The ministry seems to be depending largely on some of the propaganda we have had not only over the radio but from the Gallup poll, which seems to be galloping very fast at the present time. I think it is all gallop and no poll. It reminds me of an uncontrollable racehorse I mentioned the other night.
So far as private initiative and private enterprise are concerned, they are the key to unlocking the door of all this reconversion; they are the key to the solution of the domestic problems. You have to see the cause and effect of it. In the proposed resolution the minister refers expressly to certain orders and regulations. "By their fruits ye shall know them " The resolution speaks for itself. The minister said that on the first
Emergency Powers

reading of the proposed bill he would table certain things and schedules of the controls left. I do not wish to deal in full with the list of controls. One of them relates to a serious matter, namely, housing and all that kind of thing. The other day, the successor to the minister tabled the orders in council which are to be read into this resolution. What was it? It had to do with people and soldiers who had purchased houses up to July, 1945. At that time very few men in the army were home. In the spring of 1945 the war with Germany ended and the war with Japan ended later on in the year. In my opinion, there were few soldiers home at that time. There was a very large army overseas. Since that time they have come home. That order in council should be amended to allow soldiers into the homes they bought down to the end of 1946.
The government has no inspection services of controlled housing in regard to this housing proposition to eliminate the undesirable tenant. Under the control system there is no inspection of these houses to find out who is profiteering. Many owners have lost their homes because they could not get into them. It is leading to confiscation of property because, under the control system, under the proposed extension of these emergency powers to May 15, and under the housing matter as it stands today-I refer to an order in council passed three weeks ago-the present state of the housing situation is largely responsible for the issue of that order in council-they have done nothing to relieve the situation. The controllers have never built a single house. It is simply imposing an intolerable burden on owners of property.
I come from a city where sixty-five per cent of the people used to own their own homes. Many of them are losing them today because they cannot get into them. They rent their property to a tenant. What does he do? I have seen some houses where the tenant is profiteering, and the landlord cannot get anything out of the house. Many of the property owners have undesirable tenants who put electric stoves in cupboards and place every man they can get into small rooms with great danger to the health of the people, and break all kinds of municipal bylaws. It is leading almost to confiscation of property and insurance policies are vitiated. Nobody wants to own property under the present state of controls and taxes and continued losses on the investment. If it tended to relieve the housing situation I would not object; if it helped to get soldiers houses I would not object, but it does not.

The government spent large sums of money on public buildings. They tore down a large number of temporary huts which cost over two and half million dollars, and which were built on the waterfront in Toronto. These huts could have been used for temporary housing, but that is not being done-except to a limited extent. The army buildings are not being used to aid the housing shortage, and builders cannot get materials.
The whole story at home is told in a very few words. Are we to continue this system which is no aid to real estate? With the burden of taxation, with the housing situation as it is, with the rate of interest and taxation going up-with all these things, does it alleviate the housing situation? No; it does not. It has retarded all private enterprise and private initiative and building construction and prevented housebuilding.
In conclusion, I wish to make this point. In the United States we find an example of the grave danger from inflation that was inherent in the emergency control legislation which it was found necessary to enact during the war, but a committee was set up in Washington and they went into the whole question of controls. They adopted there, Mr. Speaker, a principle which I sincerely hope will be recognized and put into practice in Canada, under the able auspices both of yourself and of the Speaker of the senate. I hope that a joint committee of both houses of parliament will be appointed in this country to deal with these matters along the lines followed in the United States. In Washington, President Truman and some of the leaders of both houses got together and, through the medium of their ways and means committee, they have endeavoured to solve this problem in connection with controls and to decide what controls should be left to emergency legislation. There they have brought in a valuable report which indicates the dangers that exist in further controls. The result of their inquiries is that in the United States they have wiped out all controls with the exception of one or two of a minor nature, and rent matters and evictions.
Controls accomplished a great deal of good in difficult stages of the war, but now that the war has been over for two years, I hope that something will be done to eliminate them here.
I should like to read two or three sentences from the Washington Truman report, because I think it would be well for us to heed them and the warnings. I quote:
Discussing the monetary problem, the committee on monetary relations declares that "the immediate danger in most countries is now one

Emergency Powers
of continued inflation. This danger must be countered." One cause of rising prices is too much money and too much government debt; another is too little production in the face of urgent needs. The report continues;
"'To a considerable extent, the upward tendencies of prices are due to non-monetary causes, arising mainly from destruction and disorganization brought about by the war, such as the shortage of goods, deficient production, and the rising costs largely attributable to higher wages. Among the most essential tasks are an increase in the production of power, a general recovery in efficiency, and firm measures to avoid th*e vicious spiral of rising wages and prices. It should now be clear everywhere that until sufficient supplies become available, an attempt to improve the people's standard of living merely by raising money wages is doomed to failure, for it will simply lead to a rise in prices which will tend to imperil the integrity of national currencies."
But in many countries inflationary pressure is still largely the result of monetary causes in the form of large accumulations of purchasing power continually increased by deficit financing and a policy of excessively cheap money, which involves the monetization of debts and artificially increases the money valuation of capital assets.
therefore, the first task is to arrest the increase in buying power by bringing budgets under control, so that no new notes need to be printed to fill the gap between expenditure and revenue. Government expenditure must be subject to a thorough overhauling so as to eliminate superfluities and prevent too large an administrative establishment from reacting unfavourably on the budget position and on the standard of living.
I hope that we shall soon see the end of this policy of controls, which has cost the country so much. Generations yet unborn will have to pay the colossal debt that has piled up during recent years. We cannot very well appraise the situation just now. No newspaper can size it up. Historians will have to deal with it in proper perspective twenty-five years from now, and only then will the Canadian people see to their full extent what the cause and effects have been from the economic and national points of view and so far as the interests of the taxpayers and of our small businessmen are concerned, by the price ceilings, and economic controls. It is too early to predict now what the effect will be, but there is a great deal of doubt in the minds of the people today and we who are assembled here as a parliament do not seem to be doing anything to remedy the situation.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I wish to say that, contrary to the views of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and contrary also to those of the leader of the Social Credit party, I intend to speak as a Liberal and as a liberal with a small "1." It is needless, therefore, for me to state that I am in favour of controls, whether during the war or dur-83166-104
ing the period of transition from war economy to peace economy; and I am in favour of controls, I may add, for an obvious reason, that controls have proven in this war that they were serving the population at large. They were serving the small fry's interest versus the bigwig's ambitions, with the result that the people were on a standard of living in accordance with their ways and means, whereas during the first world war the big profiteers enjoyed life while the ordinary citizen did not enjoy it at all.
But I must be frank and also say at once that I am certainly not in favour of controls for the reason that was given yesterday by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) for continuing controls. The reason he gave will be found at page 1554 of Hansard of yesterday:
Great national interests are at stake in the sense that as an aftermath of the war the economic stability of the greatest national customer that this country has had in the past is endangered and it is in the national interest that food should continue to flow to the people of Great Britain in order that they may be in a position to produce goods and exchange them for our goods in the future and continue to be the great market that thev have been in the past.
I think it is about time for an enunciation of policy by the powers that be; it is about time, after the achievements of Canadians during the war just ended, for people in authority to state definitely the policy of this government and to think in Canadian terms first and always. It is about time that we minded our own business and left the interests of other people to their own countries.
I am also opposed to the way in which this resolution introduces the omnibus bill for the consideration of parliament, because I think it is the most anti-democratic and antiLiberal measure this parliament has ever seen since confederation. May I be permitted to cite authorities instead of giving my own views in this respect? I shall refer you, Mr. Speaker, to a statement made in this house by our great leader, our dear Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1932, with regard to a measure which was every bit as antidemocratic and anti-Liberal as this one is. At page 701 of Hansard, volume 1, of the session of 1932-and he was referring to chapter 58-he said:
What does this mean? Chapter 58 is the act to which I have just referred.
It was the Unemployment and Relief Act which was continued and called in 1932 the Unemployment Continuance Act.
It means that notwithstanding that parliament is in session, notwithstanding that the people's representative? ire here assembled for

Emergency Powers

the express purpose of dealing with the great problems of the country and voting supplies in the regular way, the Prime Minister-
The Prime Minister was then Mr. R. B. Bennett.
-asks this parliament to give to the ministry while parliament is in session the power to do by order in council that which should be done only by act of this parliament and by supply voted in the regular manner. A more audacious or amazing piece of legislation never was introduced to a free assembly by any prime minister. This measure proposes that, while parliament is in session, actually assembled here with representatives from all parts of the country, hon. members shall forgo, by the changing of a date in an act of parliament, their whole duty of dealing in the regular manner with the problem of unemployment in what my right hon. friend will tell us is another emergent situation.
I admit that we also are possibly in another emergent situation. But if it was that bad to introduce two objectives in one bill, I am asking you frankly what it is to introduce fifty-seven objectives. In case the Prime Minister's words are not sufficient to convince hon. members of the situation as it now stands with this omnibus bill, I shall refer the house to another hon. gentleman who at the time called himself Mr. Ilsley. At page 937 of Hansard of March 8, in the session of 1932, volume 1, I shall quote Mr. Ilsley, who is now Minister of Justice, who is introducing this resolution and who, on the bill introduced by Mr. Bennett at that time, was saying this:
I submit that the most serious objection to be taken to this resolution is that a violation of the constitutional rights of the members of this house is being sought by the government of the day. It is hard to find words strong enough to characterize the action of the government in attempting to put through this resolution. It was bad enough in the emergency session of 1930 to ask for a vote of $20,000,000 for works -which were not specified; it was worse in the session of 1931 to get from this parliament a blank cheque and legislation which set up a dictatorship between sessions, but it is infinitely worse for the government to have the temerity to come before this house and seek to perpetuate that dictatorship while parliament is in session.
I do not think I could use any better words to express myself tonight, because I think this resolution of today is quite similar to the one I refer to. I think it also involves a blank cheque, because the resolution does not indicate in any way what is the amount involved. In the second place, it is a resolution to perpetuate the sort of dictatorship which we had to stand for during the war, and which I would be willing to stand for during this period, but as a result of a resolution that should come to this house and leave in the mind of no members any doubt whatsoever as to its implications. I say that, first, with respect to money, and, second, with

regard to the controls themselves, it leaves in the minds of all members of this house nothing but doubt and suspicion. Therefore I think the words of the man who is Minister of Justice today, but who was then in opposition as the hon. member for Hants-Kings, can be easily applied to it. I said that, as far as money is concerned, we are being left in the dark. As far as the controls themselves are concerned, and the emergency power that the government is seeking in this resolution, we are advised to a certain extent of what these measures may be in this publication called "Office consolidations of orders in council, specified in the schedule to the Bill, an act to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war".
Of course I see in this things which should be dealt with and taken care of; but I also see things that we could dispense with; for instance, the breaking and separating of eggs -I do know how to break my eggs at breakfast-the pasteurizing of honey; the slaughtering and stuffing of poultry, and things of that sort. When I bring forward this criticism it is in order to seek from the minister first a rectification of the enunciation of policy that he put on Hansard yesterday for what I would call the necessity of this bill, namely, that when Britain is in need in peace time, Canada must be the cow. I would hope that when this legislation is introduced in the house and we go into it, it might be possible for the minister, instead of bringing in an omnibus bill, to break it down and separate those matters dealt with by legislation already on our statute books, and introduce new bills for other matters, as for example, with regard to the wartime prices and trade board. In any event I think it should be dealt with in such a way that all hon. members might know the amount of money involved as well as all the items included in this legislation, and their purpose.
If that is not done, I for one shall feel like a shareholder in a large corporation such as the Sun Life, the C.P.R. or some other corporation, who is called once a year to rubber-stamp the decisions of the executive. I submit to you, sir, that if that is what we are asked to do-and I say it is-there is no need for us to stay here for six months and spend the money of the taxpayers. We might as well come here for only one day and rubber-stamp the decisions of the government, or send a proxy and stay home. I do not feel that I can take the responsibility of destroying the most elementary privilege possessed

Emergency Powers
by any taxpayer of this country or any member of this house; I do not feel that I can subscribe to the annihilation of the greatest prerogative of members of the Commons by submitting to legislation twenty-five times worse than R. B. Bennett's legislation in 1931-32. I feel that I must redeem my accounts with the taxpayers of my riding and the country at large; I have to explain that when I voted for a certain bill on a certain date, I knew I was voting so much money which they would have to cough up, and that certain principles were involved touching their most intimate everyday dealings.
In conclusion, may I repeat that I hope the government will find ways and means of satisfying the people who really believe in a controlled economy, in a stabilized economy and in orderly decontrol, so that we may be in a position to vote intelligently on this legislation, and in order to give back to parliament its privileges and to members their right to know the amount of money involved and the items dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is an excellent thing for parliament to have such a prolonged discussion as this one on the matter of "controls". Among the public, it is often said that members of parliament have more or less self-control. What with hearing that said and examining the matter under its various aspects, we may come, I hope, to achieve perfect control over our thoughts, our tongues, our acts and possibly even over the present government.
It is often repeated that controls breed an over-strong and all-powerful bureaucracy. After having scrutinized the whole world and studied their political set-ups, we may very well ponder over whether any other political group represented in this house were they to attain power-and this would be their luck, not ours-would do away with this bureaucracy bred by controls, of which so much is said; whether they would do away with the civil servants, who, after all, form the only bureaucracy which has been so much talked about. I was once told, in a government department, that the civil service commission was more powerful than any government. I almost believed it, for I do not think that any party could do away entirely with bureaucracy. I do believe, however, that it would be replaced by another much stronger, more numerous and probably allpowerful.

The first price control chief was the Roman Emperor Diocletian. In the year 301 he put price ceilings on all commodities and froze wages.
On March 25, 1535, a proclamation was issued by King Henry VIII concerning butchers. It reads:
"A Proclamation Concerning Butchers 1535" Dated this 25 of March of reign of King Henry the VIII
Forasmuch as the King's Majesty is credibly advertised and informed, that beeves, muttons, and veals are likely to be more scarce and dear now against this holy time of Easter than in other seasons of the year, by reason of the charges of keeping such cattle with hay and other stover in the winter; by occasion whereof the butchers and others that shall sell such beeves, muttons, and veals by weight cannot buy them of the breeders, brokers, farmers, drovers, owners, and feeders of such cattle at such reasonable prices in gross as they may sell the same again by weight by retail at such prices as are limited in the act made for selling of flesh by weight, unless it should be to their utter loss and undoing; His Highness therefore willing that the same butchers and others selling flesh by retail for the time hereafter limited in this proclamation should be so conveniently provided for in the premises as they should not have any cause reasonably to forebear their provisions for such victuals to be sold at retail against this holy time of Easter for relief and succor of his subjects in as ample manner as heretofore have been accustomed; is therefore contented and pleased that, from henceforth until the 23rd day of June next coming, butchers and all others that shall sell flesh of the kinds aforesaid by weight by retail shall and may sell from time to time, unto the said 23rd day of June next coming, every pound of beef good and wholesome for man's body for a half-penny and one halffarthing and no more:	And every pound of
mutton for three farthings only and no more. And every pound of veal for a half-penny and half farthing and no more. The said act of provision heretofore had and made for selling flesh by weight by retail, or anything therein contained, to the contrary hereof notwithstanding.
Provided always that no butcher or others shall kill any calves to sell by retail for the term of two years ensuing, from the first day of January last, upon the pains limited in the act made for killing of calves, this proclamation notwithstanding. And his Highness hath ordained that if any butcher or others selling by retail do sell any of the kinds of victuals aforesaid otherwise than by weight or at any priecs than is afore limited or refuse to sell according to this proclamation; then every butcher or others so offending shall suffer loss and forfeit all such pains and penalties and also be ordered in all

things as is contained and limited in the act made for the. premises. This proclamation in any wise not letting.
And furthermore the King's Highness straightly chargeth and eommandeth all and every one of the said breeders, brokers, drovers, feeders, farmers, and owners of such cattle that they and every one of them furnish the fairs and markets with such fat cattle as they have to sell from time to time in as large and ample a manner as hath been the custom:	And to sell
their said cattle at such reasonable prices as the said butchers or such others as shall retail the same again by w'eight may utter and sell the same to his loving subjects at such prices as are above limited, as they will avoid his Grace's high displeasure and answer to the same at their uttermost perils.
And that after the said 23rd day of June, the said butchers and others selling flesh by retail shall from thenceforth sell by weight by retail according to the prices limited in the same act and made and provided for the same upon the pains and penalties contained in the said act without any abstinence or redress to be had thereof after the said 23rd day. Wherefore the King's Highness straightly chargeth and eommandeth all the singular mayors, justices of peace, sheriffs, bailiffs, constables, and other his officers and faithful subjects to whom it shall or in any manner or wise appertain that they and every one cause this his proclamation to be put in due and effectual execution according to the tenor thereof, as they will answer to his Highness at their uttermost perils.

Mr. Speaker, controls are merely the result of war, or at any rate, of an unusual situation, Ever since I have been sitting on this side of the house and even during the two long sessions when I sat on the other side, we were wont to say that our war effort would have a most disturbing effect on the economy of this country if it did not destroy it. Obviously, at that time, without presuming to prophesy, we feared that the war effort would be too great and that it would result in coercive measures being applied during and after the end of hostilities.
Controls are coercive measures and nobody likes them; they do not please any mother of a family or charitable institutions; nor do they please old people or children who are thereby deprived of some of the necessaries of life, but since the child is born-"control" -it must be brought up and be it a matter of controls, price regulations or something else, we must put up with everything on account of the present economic situation not only in Canada but throughout the world, and that is the point we must consider.

Emergency Powers
Let us take as an example the rationing of sugar. It did not please anyone. Everyone likes sugar, and more especially children, sick and elderly people who need it most. It was absolutely necessary to ration sugar because, since 1942, production was altogether insufficient.
The output of North America, the continent in which we live, amounted in 1938 to 2,467,258 tons of sugar, while in 1946, it had dropped to 1,845,000 tons, which means an annual reduction of at least 600,000 tons. That, however, is nothing compared with Europe which was laid waste by war. Its annual sugar output of 9,412,325 tons in 1938 decreased through the years to 5,700,000 tons in 1946. Therefore, war-torn Europe needs some of these controls and rigid rationing must be maintained so that world-wide distribution may be adequate.
Take Asia, for instance. Production has decreased by 2,380,255 tons, a drop which is almost as disastrous as that which occurred in Europe. If you multiply these figures by the number of years included between 1942 and 1946, you will see how inadequately the sugar output compares with demand and consumption.
Now, I come to the Philippines which have been almost destroyed by the Japanese. The production there, in 1938, amounted to 1,039,305 tons, while, in 1946, it had fallen to 13,000 tons. Listen to this: in Java, production, in 1938, was 1,761,000 tons and only 125,000 tons, in 1947. You can see the difference right there and realize at the same time that rationing is not entirely bad, especially in regard to certain goods, such as those I am speaking about at this moment, and which must first be distributed, if we are at all human, to those who need them, those whose health is failing, who are advanced in age and must have a definite amount of calories to keep alive.
In Formosa, the same conditions prevail. Production, which stood at 1,487,000 tons in 1938, is estimated at only 175,000 tons for this year. Fortunately, Europe is recovering faster than the Philippines, Java, Formosa and Borneo, for the Europeans had foreseen that they could some day be short of sugar, either as a consequence of war or of some other catastrophe and they put in larger acreages in sugar beets.
This reminds me first of having heard the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), in 1942, delivering a speech, requesting the government to encourage the growing of sugar-beets. I also remember that, in 1932, while a member of the provincial legislature, the hon. member for Montmagny, Mr. Paquette, a former mayor of the City of Quebec, the hon. member for Quebec Centre,
Mr. Samson and myself had initiated a debate on sugar-beet growing. We had not much success then, but today the province of Quebec is equipped with a beet plant of 1,200 ton daily capacity at St. Hilaire. Other sugar-beet factories in various parts of the country, including Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario, have a daily capacity of 11,200 tons. I submit that if, in anticipation of some accident, or rather of such a scourge as war, we had developed the sugar-beet industry to a greater extent, as Europe has, we would have suffered less hardships from sugar rationing because we would have been in a better position to cope with our requirements.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that controls are depressing and irritating. We dislike them, as everybody else, except those who believe in state regimentation. Even though we may not fancy this liberal enactment, let us consider the present situation in Canada and outside the country. At the beginning of the war, I spoke the following words in this house:
In order to survive, democracy will have to resort eventually to the very same means which are used against it if it hopes to conquer enemies bent upon its destruction.
Totalitarians resorted to controls in Germany, Russia, Spain and elsewhere. Why? To regulate their expenses, their production, their consumption in order to reach a goal of which they never lost sight: the domination of the whole world and the destruction of true democracy. I was justified, and I still am, in saying that even if it does not please our constituents democracies must sometimes resort to the very means used against them by their opponents. I quote a recent article from the New York Herald Tribune-.
Canada has shown us how to control salaries and prices during the war and now apparently she shows us the way in which controls must be lifted during the reconversion period.
I understand that some people demand the immediate abolition of controls. However, I find with dismay that those who demanded a superhuman war effort of Canada, knowing that the expenditures entailed would endanger our economy, are the ones who clamour for the lifting of controls and the return to peace-time conditions.
And now, we are labouring under the very conditions brought about by the pressure they exerted at that time. Canada gradually reduces her staffs. The number of employees of the prices board has shrunk by 1,220 in 1946 and further cuts are contemplated. I do not claim to be more liberal than anyone else, and I do not intend to give the impression that I changed my mind when
Emergency Powers

I took a seat among the liberals; I still hold to the same opinions which I held and voiced at that time, when I stated that controls were things that we could hardly countenance and that we abhorred even. However, we foresaw that the state of war and Canada's war effort, as well as that of all the countries of the world, would bring about the conditions under which we are presently labouring. If we study the schedule of prices referred to, yesterday, by the Right Hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) in his review, we find that the United States have experienced a disastrous and frightful rise in prices as a result of having removed all controls at one stroke. Those who will read the statement of the Right Hon. the Minister of Justice will see that the controls, in Canada were not done away with all at once, which has certainly been to the advantage of the Canadian economy and the Canadian taxpayer.
Mr. Speaker, that it is proper to quote in this connection a statement which the right honourable the Prime Minister made early in February. It reads as follows:
The Tories would abolish in one fell swoop all government controls. The socialists of the C.C.F. would not only maintain them, but multiply them and establish them permanently. The Liberals avoid those two extremes; they want neither to abolish the controls for the benefit of private interests nor extend them needlessly, but keep those which certain circumstances make necessary in the .general interest.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, like all the hon. members who have spoken before, I cannot accept straight away and smilingly a system of controls which will continue to be enforced. Some of those controls have been abolished and others will be. I hope that all will disappear in the near future. But, while I am not and do not pretend to be an economist, I cannot see how any country in the world, can possibly remove all controls on its domestic and its external trade.
That is why I shall vote for the bill, even though I do not like it. This does not mean that I have changed my mind about those measures of control, it is merely because I feel that we must keep a certain degree of control so that our economy will not be entirely destroyed, especially in view of the hard blows it has suffered after the war.

Quite a bit has been said about the south end on the government side. Since I represent the extreme south of the south end

I feel at times as though I were in Antarctica -I must express my views. I am afraid I

cannot say it is a solid south at the present time, because I shall have to differ with my good friend the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote).
I am one who is convinced that this omnibus bill should go through as quickly as possible. I wish to explain at the outset that I am a Liberal, a Liberal of the Liberals, and I do not like controls as such. But I realize that there are times when we have to exercise controls, when we are in an emergency; and we are definitely in an emergency now. It is true that the guns have ceased firing, but we are going through possibly a more difficult period from the economic point of view than when the guns were still firing. We are running into what I consider to be the final lap, and if we falter in that lap and lose the race as a result of trying to be too hasty I maintain that we shall live to regret it.
We are not the only country which has to exercise controls. I had not expected to speak on this resolution; I had intended to wait until we came to second reading of the bill, but because the south end of the house has been referred to so often I thought I had better express my view's. I picked up the Halifax Herald of March 20 while sitting here, and what do I see. The date line is "Washington, March 19-AP". I will not read the whole item. The heading is "Ask Power be Continued." I quote:
President Truman asked congress today to continue his wartime power to control shipments abroad, as a curb on inflation at home and as a tool to help those countries "whose existence must be preserved".
Further on I read:
Uncontrolled shipments into the higher-priced markets abroad would encourage domestic inflation and increase "the already substantial burden of living costs borne by the American people."
I skip a paragraph and read the last:
About 500 items, mostly foods, now are under export curbs, compared with a war-time total of more than 3,000. Truman promised the fastest possible removal of controls but predicted that the need for them will "remain acute for some time".
I maintain that our position is very similar to the position over there, only we are much better off inasmuch as we have never relinquished controls in the wholesale manner in which they did in the United States and for which they are suffering today. I would urge all hon. members not to treat this question on party lines. It is too important for that. We want to get rid of these controls as soon as we can, but we must regard this as a big measure which we must face for a limited period of time.

Emergency Powers
We have been operating safely under these controls under the wartime prices and trade board and I contend that we have nothing to fear by operating under them for a few months longer. But we have a good deal to fear if we do not get this legislation through in sufficient time.
The suggestion has been made that we have separate bills for all fifty-five items. That would be all right if we had the time; but from what I have seen in this house this session, I suggest that, by the time we got through, the need for control would have gone by or the holocaust would have caught up with us and we would be definitely out of luck. We have not time to do it. We have to recognize that fact. Therefore I urge that as soon as we possibly can, when members have expressed what opinions they may have, we allow the Speaker to leave the chair so that we can consider the matter in committee.

Until now the question has been
put whether one is for or against controls. Some have said they do not like controls, and it is a respectable opinion. They have said also that, although they do not like controls, they would be in favour of continuing them for the public good. That is acceptable. Some others have been against. It was their view and also mine, and I wonder if my hon. friend the member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), who has just spoken, had in view those who have expressed themselves against controls when he passed such severe judgment against them. I wonder if his words apply to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and to my humble self.

They apply
to no one in particular.

All of us together.
Therefore he divided the house into two categories, those who see the light and those who do not. I appreciate the fact that he has the right to his own views.

I never
meant that.

No, but it is my understanding of what the hon. member said. There is no one who is more ready to concede that everyone has a perfect right to his own view. Well, the question may be put differently. One may be for the controls in principle; but under certain conditions, one may be for the controls theoretically but against the application of the controls. These distinctions are necessary in a discussion. In the first place, I would be in favour of controls 83166-105
-and in fact I -was the first one who wired to the Prime Minister on the eve of the war to ask him to see to it that prices of sugar and flour would not rise too quickly-under one or several cabinet ministers responsible to the House of Commons, responsible to parliament. That kind of control I would be for in case of emergency.
I believe that parliament is supreme and I believe also it is a great mistake to establish boards or commissions that are entirely independent of the government. If they are created as independent of the government it is because of the intellectual laziness and lack of determination of the members of the cabinet who would not assume responsibility for unpopular measures taken by a board in charge of control. It is just as clear as spring water. And then the control is decided; independent boards are organized, and members of parliament are just rubber-stamps to vote measures like this one.
Mostly soft rubber.

That is another respectable opinion. Therefore, sir, I am against the constitution of commissions and boards that are independent of the government. It is precisely the view of the C.C.F. socialist party to have such boards organized and manned by men who are superior to members of parliament taken as a whole. These men on the boards-I am not complaining of anyone in particular; I am considering the question on principle-are considered superior to members of parliament, and we are here to give them powers which we are afraid to discharge. That is the constitution of all the boards that we have.
But there is something else. We are at the other end of the line. No minister has the outlook that a private member of parliament has on the effect of any legislation because, in the first place, ministers are not in daily contact with their constituents and because, in the second place, most of their constituents do not write to them except to ask for special favours. At times it may be letters of friendship, but when a man does not live among his constituents for the greater part of the year he loses contact with them. Moreover, ministers are surrounded by men who tell them that the wrong thing is the right thing and when a member of parliament tells them the truth it is sometimes considered as heresy.
If controls are necessary they should be under one or several members of the cabinet; then I am sure my hon. friend, who voted against controls on Bill No. 25 and on another occasion, would accept controls because, when

Emergency Powers

the question of controls would come before the house, the minister would have to give explanations just the same as he gives in connection with any matter coming under his department. What I regret very much is that those who man the control boards very often consider themselves infallible. They think that if they admit a mistake they are doing something they should not do and they will be ashamed of themselves. They are not supposed to err. They are the infallible ones. Therefore, when it is pointed out to them that there is something wrong somewhere, they will not admit it, for any reason. Then the minister will tell us that it is difficult for him to intervene in such a case because he would not want to intervene in regard to an independent board. How is it that those people are independent? They have grown up like mushrooms, and it is impossible for members of parliament to make any observations to them. Sometimes we may make observations and explain certain things to them. As I said to one of them the other day, and as I said just a minute ago, members of parliament are the shock-absorbers. They are the other end of the line. We know what is going wrong with the application of controls, and we very often tell them that there is some-redressed, to have the error corrected so that the people of the country will not complain of any injustice. It is evident that the controls are unpopular. They cannot be popular. But they should be exercised with fairness so that no one can complain of any injustice at the hands of any officers of any branch.
It is necessary to keep order in the country and to maintain the respect of the Canadian people for our institutions. But what happened in my constituency? There was an overzealous man who was closely related to one of the members of the wartime prices and trade board, and who was in charge of an office in my county. He was unjust to the people. I will not say that he was dishonest, but I wall say that he was unjust. He even went so far as to put the people under oath and ask them what price they had paid for used cars? I brought those facts before the board, but I did not get a satisfactory reply. I wanted that man to be fired, but he was never fired because he had support in high places. Finally, at the request of the wardens and the mayors of the county, the office was closed. I asked that the office be closed just in order to get rid of one incompetent man, and what did I discover afterwards? I discovered that the man was in the Quebec office and to a large extent in charge of the business for the twenty-three counties in the district

of Quebec. It is impossible to get rid of them. He was like a girl who was employed in the civil service. She missed her examinations nine times and was fired at my request. The first news that the civil service commission had was that her chief had protested against her being fired, saying that she was rendering exceptional service. It is the same thing with regard to these people I speak of. We cannot get rid of them.
Is it not possible to make a certain cleanup in all these controls? There is great duplication. There are controls in the Department of Reconstruction; there are controls in the prices board, besides the control of the treasury and the foreign exchange control board. There are controls everywhere. There are fences. There are ropes. There are all kinds of ways to keep the people embarrassed and inactive. I will suggest something to the minister before the bill comes out, but I wonder if it will be of any use because the whole bill may be cooked now. However I will put it on record and show my willingness to help by making a few suggestions. Why not get rid of the controls of the wartime prices and trade board, which duplicate those that exist in the Department of Reconstruction? Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) told us that in the Department of Agriculture they established floor prices, but the ceiling prices were established by the wartime prices and trade board. If controls are necessary, why not have the ceiling prices of agricultural products established by the Department of Agriculture or by the Minister of Agriculture; and under his authority, so that he will be responsible for the matter in parliament? That is one suggestion. The same thing applies to all departments.
Instructions have been given to reduce the staff of all departments by ten per cent, to fire mostly minor employees such as stenographers, clerks, messengers, and so on. Why not dispense with the useless, dead branches of duplication? It is easy to do.
I will not speak much longer, sir, because all the discussions which are carried on in the house, even when fine and eloquent speeches are made, are purely academic. There is no result. I remember one day that six members of parliament obtained what they wanted by uniting; and the matter in point was not one of national importance. It concerned steel pipes. There were six members-one was from British Columbia, another from Winnipeg and I do not remember where the others were from-who joined together to call on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, and complain about the high price, or the

Emergency Powers
increase of price by the prices board with regard to steel pipes. It was not a matter of national importance, but they went there and said to them, "Gentlemen, if you do not reduce those prices to what they were before, we will vote against you." They obtained what they wanted. Everything was all right and the prices were changed, although it had been found by the prices board that the prices were too high.
I have not always had the support that I expected to have on matters of public interest, and although I respect the opinions of others I do not despair of the future, because in a matter of minor importance last year the House of Commons was turned upside down by the new members on the question of whether we would have Canada day or Dominion day, a matter of very little importance. But the senate argued for weeks and months about it. They did not know whether it should be Canada day or Dominion day. Why discuss it? We must have Dominion day; there is no reason for having Canada day when there is one single member who is against it and who prefers Dominion day as a sign of colonialism. But here in the house one vote was 26 to 165, and among the twenty-six were thirteen cabinet ministers, while among the 165 were two cabinet ministers. All votes were most interesting. The discussion lasted a day. Although it concerned a matter of minor importance, everybody was concerned about it, and the rank and file won the day in the House of Commons, which shows that we can expect something for the future if members first know what they want and then unite for that particular purpose. It was done last year. It could be done today in matters of greater importance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We also had a vote last year on the price of milk.
Exactly, and it was forgotten very quickly, unfortunately.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not by the people.

I will not say by the people. The vote was significant but the result was nil. I regretted not being in the house that day, because I would have voted with my hon. friends. I arrived in the evening, and that occurred in the afternoon. But it was well done. The hon. member who has just spoken got a promise, but if I am not mistaken that promise turned out to mean nothing. With regard to the Canada day business the House of Commons did its duty; then the Senate was all mixed up; finally the legislation stayed on the table and we did not hear of it again. It is a question of peace, of not 83166-105*
drawing a red herring across the trail, of being quiet and good in order not to hurt those who think we should continue to have Dominion day instead of Canada day. We can carry on like that in regard to various small matters, but when the time comes to discuss important matters it seems to me the essential distinction is not made between important matters and minor questions.
I do not despair of the future. I still hope for a better future, but we shall have it only if men who have a definite purpose unite and follow the example of those who were so successful in having the price of steel pipes reduced to what it was before, and if the members of the house will continue to do as well for public business as they did for Canada day last year. Am I right or wrong to hope for a better future? It all depends upon my colleagues. More than that, sir, I believe the distinction between political parties is a pure farce. I am a Liberal at heart and proud of it, but I do not see how a Liberal could stand for a socialist measure like this control by independent boards. I am bitterly opposed to it. Control under the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley); control under the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott); control under any minister responsible to parliament; that is one thing. The Minister of Justice is responsible to parliament for the mounted police. He brings in a report. That is all right; I do not complain about it. But everything should be like that. Now we must admit we have been remiss in our duty by not making the necessary distinctions and by letting those mushrooms grow in such numbers that the government and even the House of Commons- because the government is no worse than the house-are afraid to abolish these controls. Why not replace them by controls responsible to parliament, so that members of parliament will have their say; so that members of parliament will be heard when they make representations on behalf of the taxpayers of this country who happen to be their constituents and who are entitled to justice from anyone.
I wonder how many hon. members have read the resolution sponsored by the Minister of Justice. It reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war-
Mark this, sir.
-and to provide therein that the governor in council may appoint and fix the compensation of the officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of any older or regulation continued in force bv the act-
Emergency Powers

That is the first thing. The second is:
-and further to provide that certain officers, clerks and employees may continue to perform the duties for which they were previously appointed.
In the first place, we are to have the creation of new boards and commissions; there are not enough already. In the second place, provision is made for the continuation of the present state of affairs. Then, how are we to reduce bureaucracy? We are creating more and more bureaucrats all the time. Bill No. 25 created more boards, more advisers, more men who will come from outside to supplant parliament, more termites who will destroy the pillars of the state, and now we are to have still more and more. Nearly everybody is for it, and there are philosophical dissertations about controls. "We like them". "We don't like them". "We think they are necessary". "We think they are not necessary", and no action is taken. I believe in the sincerity of all my colleagues who are so kind to me, but may I tell them that my faith will be greater the day members unite to interview the government and, notify them they will cease their support if they do not make necessary changes, and if we do not have responsible instead of irresponsible controls.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution now
before the house is simply the continuation of the administrations, controls and plans set up on account of the war.
The war ended in 1945, almost two years age, and the "plan makers" are still trying to persuade the people that the continuation of control measures is necessary and that their abolition would be detrimental to the economic stability of Canada. Where, in 1947, is economic stability to be found in our country? Strikes are going on across the country, production has sharply decreased and our wealth and available products are very unequally distributed. Black markets are rampant all over the country and we wonder why they should exist in Canada. Why were there no black markets in 1939 and how is it they exist in 1947? Why did they exist during the war? It is easy, very easy, to understand. In 1939, we had not controls, whereas these controls exist in 1947, as they did during the war. Therefore, these controls are the cause of black markets. How can we do away with black markets unless we begin by abolishing controls? In order to illustrate what I have in mind, I should like to read to the house an article which appeared in the newspaper Vers Demain. edition of March 1, 1947, under the title: "Subsidies vs. controls."
When stores are full but pockets empty, the unsold goods remain outside the home. One recalls the depression, when neither dealers nor customers were satisfied. When pockets are full but stores empty, non-existent goods remain outside the home. Such is too often the ease today, when neither dealers nor customers are satisfied.
What applies to dealers and customers is also true of landlords and tenants, since houses are goods, and equally so of doctors and patients, since professional services provide for certain needs.
Therefore, two conditions are required:
First, the goods must exist.
Second, consumers must have money to pay for the goods.
In other words, we have on the one side goods and money on the other, that is farmers, industrialists, workers of all kinds, who produce abundantly and buyers who pay well.
How can the first condition be met? Through an ever-expanding production of consumer goods of which Canada has already proved herself capable.
Everything that encourages production helps to produce goods. Everything that discourages production tends to cause shortages.
When do we encourage production?
When we enable the producer to sell his goods at a profitable price.
When do we discourage production?
When we prevent the producer from selling his products or when we compel him to sell them at an unprofitable price.
Who should determine the selling price?
The seller because he knows how much his products cost him.
A reasonable selling price includes the cost of production plus an adequate margin of profit. Only the dealer or the producer are in a position to determine the selling price. They cannot sell at a loss; if they do, they cannot earn a living. They cannot demand prohibitive prices, otherwise their competitors will undersell them.
What happens when the wartime prices board in Ottawa determines the prices of goods throughout the country? Every producer who for that reason must sell at a loss or without profit first decreases his production, hoping to better is before long; if the system lasts, he finally sells his cattle or his farm, his machinery or his factory. As a result, goods cease to flow toward the market.
Do controls therefore cause production to drop? Certainly, as experience has proved. Before controls came into being, everything was plentiful. Since they have been brought into effect, any number of products are in short supply.
Free enterprise, unhampered by dictatorial boards and their inspectors, has always been capable of mass production. Controls, state-management, have not only shackled freedom but have also hindered production.
How can plentiful supply be brought back? By the removal of controls set up because of the war.
Will the lifting of controls not cause prices to increase? Yes, rents and the price of various commodities will rise to a level which will bring profits to owners and producers, which is quite normal. That is needed to bring back plentiful supply and widespread house building projects.
